newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico election looks cleaner but fraud fears persist.
newsitem.headline: Mexico election looks cleaner but fraud fears persist.

text.p: Crucial mid-term elections next week are expected to be Mexico's cleanest yet, political observers say, though vivid memories of past frauds mean fears of foul play persist.

Years of electoral manipulation under the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) reached its apogee in 1988 with what many Mexicans believe was the fictitious result of the presidential election.

First results put the opposition ahead, then the computer counting the votes mysteriously crashed. When it came back, the PRI was winning. Ballot papers from the election were then burned to prevent independent investigation.
But inch-by-inch constitutional reforms since then have shut many chinks in the system for rigging the July 6 vote.
"There is not the remotest possibility of fraud," Jose Woldenberg, president of Mexico's newly independent Federal Electoral Institute (IFE), told reporters this week.
PRI President Humberto Roque Villaneuva has denied that voters could be hoodwinked this time and Interior Minister Emilio Chauyffet has promised "totally clean" elections.
Mexicans will be voting for a new lower house of Congress, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and for the first time this century, Mexico City's mayor.
Polls show the PRI will lose Mexico City and may be robbed of its lower house Congress majority for the first time.
But the principal opposition parties -- the right-wing National Action Party (PAN), and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) -- still have some concerns.

"We are very accustomed to electoral violations," said Rafael Hernandez, the PRD's deputy director for electoral affairs based in Mexico City. "These elections are very competitive and we fear the PRI candidates will be tempted to undertake fraudulent activities."
Afraid the PRI will intimidate electors about to cast their vote, the PRD and the PAN are joining forces in sending monitors to many of the country's 104,000 polling stations.
IFE says 250 foreign visitors -- in nationalist Mexico they are not called electoral observers -- have applied to monitor the poll.
But the opposition warns that 25,000 polling booths in remote country areas are especially vulnerable to pressure on polling day.

A key change has been the decision in 1996 to grant the IFE, previously a branch of the Interior Ministry, independence from the government. But opposition parties are not convinced all its officials are impartial.
"It is very difficult to have open fraud but we have a few doubts about some members of the IFE," a PAN spokesman said.
Workers casting their ballots on oil rigs in the Gulf of Mexico have pressed the PRD for reassurance that their votes will actually reach the counting stations.
And already in Mexico's southern Campeche state the PRD has reported the discovery by two carpenters of illicit ballot papers in the apartment of a PRI official.
But so far such incidents appear isolated in comparison to the scale of past frauds.

IFE says the chance of vote-rigging tactics, like "pregnant ballot boxes" and "tacos" -- ballots stuffed with extra, fake votes -- is remote since the boxes themselves have been redesigned to collapse if tampered with.
To prevent the dead from voting, Mexico's 52 million voters must show photographic identification cards, which are checked against a master list with photos, before casting their ballots.
Each elector will make a thumb print in indellible ink that should make double voting impossible.
Public confidence in the elections has improved dramatically since the 1988 "computer crash." A poll this week showed that only 35.5 percent of voters mistrusted the IFE.
